Sauces / Heritage

Classic Ssamjang

The savory fermented-paste dip that belongs within reach of every lettuce wrap.

Korean · Easy · Makes about 250 g (a table's bowl)

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 05 / 5 sauces recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the table's oldest assembly. Ssamjang — literally "wrap sauce" — is the bowl that makes a grill table a ssam table: doenjang and gochujang in one paste, sweetened, studded with aromatics, sitting between the meat and the lettuce with an authority no bottled sauce matches. It is less a recipe than a ratio with every household's thumbprint on it; this record is the classic center from which the variations swing. Every meat record on this site points here, and the bowl takes ten minutes.

The base
The aromatics (the part that separates table-made from jarred)

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Nothing cooks in the classic build — the order is the technique. Work the doenjang and gochujang together first with the honey and sesame oil until the two pastes are one color (a minute of real stirring; lumps of pure doenjang in the bowl are the amateur tell), then the pear and its juice, then garlic, scallion, and seeds last so they stay bright.
  • Taste on a lettuce leaf, not a spoon: the leaf's water and bitterness are part of the sauce's final context. On the leaf it should read deep-savory first, sweet second, a slow warm hum behind.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Blend the base: doenjang, gochujang, honey, sesame oil, worked to one uniform rust color. Checkpoint — no light-brown streaks; one paste.
  2. 02
    The pear in with its juice, the splash of mirin, then garlic, scallions, sesame. Fold to a spreadable paste — looser than jam, thicker than a dressing; it must cling to a lettuce leaf without pooling. Checkpoint — the raw-build taste test on the leaf: salty-fermented depth, pear's lift, garlic's bite, the scallion still crisp. This is the bowl.
  3. 03
    The cooked build (optional, for a mellower bowl): the blended paste simmered in a lightly oiled pan 3–4 minutes with a splash of water — the garlic rounds, the gochujang's raw edge cooks off, and the sauce keeps a day longer. The raw bowl is brighter; the cooked bowl is deeper; both are classic, and the choice is the table's. Checkpoint — the cooked build darkens a shade and smells toasted rather than sharp — pull it before the sugars catch (medium-low, stirring, no crisping). Chef’s Note — the ratio is a dial, and knowing the dial is knowing the dish: more doenjang runs the bowl deep and mild (the family table's build); more gochujang runs it hot and sweet (the drinking table's); the pear amount is the freshness dial that both camps steal from each other. The jarred ssamjang at the market is the same idea pre-dialed to the middle — it is a fine start, and the ten-minute upgrade is the aromatics: fresh garlic, scallion, and grated pear into the jar's paste takes it most of the way to this bowl.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Too saltyDoenjang-forward buildMore pear and honey; a teaspoon of water
One-note heatGochujang-forward buildA spoon of doenjang to floor it
Bitter aftertasteGarlic overwhelmed the bowl or burnt (cooked build)Half the garlic; medium-low with stirring
Watery, runs off the leafOver-loosenedLet it stand 10 minutes; the pear's juice thickens it

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Raw build keeps 3–4 days refrigerated; the cooked build a week. The bowl actually improves overnight as the pear and garlic marry — make it the morning of the grill.
  • Variations: a spoon of crushed walnuts (the picnic build); chopped kimchi brine-folded for the funk table; a teaspoon of miso in place of a third of the doenjang for a sweeter, rounder bowl — labeled as the fusion fork.
